summary: Take control of a rover and explore four real regions of the Red Planet. Cross canyons, craters, ice caps and the tallest volcano in the solar system, analyze science samples, uncover a network of underground tunnels and retrace the real route of the NASA Perseverance rover.
details:
Mars · Terrain Simulator & Interplanetary Survival Guide

Team: Isabelinos Espaciales

1. What does it do or how does it work?

The project combines an Interplanetary Survival and Logistics Guide with an Interactive 3D Martian Exploration Simulator accessible directly from a web browser with no installation required.

At a functional level, users take control of a 6-wheeled rover equipped with a rocker-bogie suspension and realistic physics—including Martian surface gravity ($3.71\text{ m/s}^2$), jumping, chassis tilt aligned with terrain normals, and solar power management—to explore four procedurally generated real regions of Mars: Valles Marineris, Gale Crater, North Pole (Ice cap and dunes), and Olympus Mons.

The simulator integrates two mission modes and advanced mechanics:

  • Science Sampling Mission: Users locate and analyze 5 geological targets per region—such as lakebed clays,hydrated minerals, $\text{CO}_2$ frost, and lava tubes—triggering real scientific facts from NASA missions upon completing each sample analysis.
  • Perseverance Route Mission (Mars 2020): A scaled reconstruction ($\approx 1:112$) of the NASA Perseverance rover's historic traverse in Jezero Crater using real NASA areographic coordinates: from Octavia E. Butler Landing($18.4447^\circ\text{ N}, 77.4508^\circ\text{ E}$) to Neretva Vallis ($18.55^\circ\text{ N}, 77.20^\circ\text{ E}$),passing through Three Forks and the Bright Angel formation (where the Cheyava Falls rock with potential biosignatures was discovered).
  • Atmospheric and Subsurface Simulation: Users can switch in real time between four Martian weather presets (clear, dust storm, blue sunset, and night with Phobos and Deimos overhead) and toggle an X-ray subsurface radar view to descend via an access shaft into an explorable underground tunnel network 12 meters below the surface.

2. What benefits does it offer?

  • Democratization and immediate accessibility: By evolving from a desktop prototype into a lightweight, self-contained single-file web application (index.html), any student, educator, or space enthusiast can explore Mars from a standard browser without installing specialized software or requiring high-end hardware.
  • Immersive learning grounded in real NASA data: Transforms complex geographic, atmospheric, and astrobiological datasets into a hands-on experience, linking live rover telemetry (coordinates, elevation, temperature,sol counter, and Local Mean Solar Time—LMST) directly to the scientific context of each discovery.
  • Logistics planning and hazard analysis: Serves as a visual support tool to understand mobility constraints along Martian transit corridors (such as the route connecting Olympus Mons, Amazonis Planitia, and Valles Marineris),demonstrating the operational value of underground shelters against ionizing radiation and dust storms.
  • Bilingual reach: Features native support and instant switching between English and Spanish, broadening its educational impact for international audiences.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • STEM education and public outreach: Foster scientific curiosity and interest in space exploration by allowing students to experience firsthand how NASA robotic missions operate, while illustrating counterintuitive Martian phenomena such as blue sunsets caused by fine atmospheric dust scattering and nocturnal temperature drops below $-80^\circ\text{C}$.
  • Awareness of human and robotic exploration challenges: Highlight the real physical constraints that govern habitat design, vehicle engineering, and life-support logistics on Mars—including low atmospheric pressure,abrasive regolith containing toxic perchlorates, crew isolation, and Earth–Mars communication delays.
  • Extensible foundation for prototype simulation: Its modular architecture provides a baseline for future iterations integrating telemetry from low-cost terrestrial COTS rovers (e.g., Raspberry Pi-based prototypes) and route-reconnaissance workflows inspired by the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter.

4. What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

The project followed an iterative two-stage engineering workflow:

  • Phase 1 – Desktop Prototype (a-marte.py): Built in Python using the Ursina Engine to validate procedural terrain generation algorithms (2D fractal noise, craters, canyons, and dunes), basic rover physics, and atmospheric lighting presets.
  • Phase 2 – 3D Web Simulator (index.html): Migrated and expanded using JavaScript (ES Modules), HTML5, and CSS3 powered by Three.js (WebGL). Key implementations include custom GLSL shaders for atmospheric sky scattering, soft shadow mapping (PCFSoftShadowMap), procedural regolith textures generated via HTML5 Canvas 2D, particle systems for airborne dust storms, and a real-time telemetry HUD with a dynamic compass and topographic minimap.
  • Data sources and scientific documentation: Public NASA mission datasets (MOLA/Mars Global Surveyor, Mars 2020/Perseverance, Curiosity, Viking, InSight, and Ingenuity) used to parameterize areographic coordinates,altitudes, thermal ranges, and atmospheric composition.
  • Deployment: Static web hosting via GitHub

5. How is your project creative?

  • Blending scientific rigor with zero-friction web gamification: Rather than delivering a static map or an isolated technical report, the project translates real Perseverance coordinates and Martian geophysical parameters into a playable, interactive 3D environment packaged inside a single self-contained HTML file.
  • Scaled cartographic projection over procedural biomes: The team engineered a local equirectangular projection that scales Perseverance's multi-kilometer traverse across Jezero Crater ($\approx 1:112$) so users can drive and retrace the mission continuously over any of the four simulated Martian terrains.
  • Dual surface-to-subsurface exploration: Incorporating an X-ray terrain toggle and a functional elevator shaft leading into an illuminated underground tunnel network creatively visualizes survival strategies against radiation and global dust storms, connecting habitat engineering directly to gameplay.

6. What factors did your team take into account?

  • Real geophysical and environmental parameters: Modeled Martian surface gravity ($3.71\text{ m/s}^2$), diurnal and nocturnal temperature swings ($-20^\circ\text{C}$ down to $-80^\circ\text{C}$), atmospheric opacity during dust storms, and the accumulation of water ice and $\text{CO}_2$ frost at high elevations and polar latitudes.
  • Topography and navigation hazards: Accounted for terrain-specific mobility risks—such as basal escarpments around Olympus Mons, smooth sedimentary plains, polar dunes, and tectonic canyons like Valles Marineris—reflecting them in rover chassis pitch/roll dynamics and dangerous slope warnings ($>30^\circ$).
  • Energy management and survival constraints: Implemented a power drain and solar-recharging model sensitive to weather and depth: solar panels recharge at full efficiency under clear daylight, drop sharply during dust storms or sunset, and cease charging at night or underground, triggering low-power emergency speed limits and automatic headlights.
  • Historical and astrobiological accuracy: Verified official NASA coordinates for Mars 2020 milestones—correcting common database discrepancies regarding the northern latitude of Neretva Vallis—and incorporated the scientific context of Cheyava Falls and its "leopard spot" mineral reaction fronts (vivianite and greigite).
  • Performance and usability: Optimized geometry rendering (instanced rocks, lightweight procedural textures, and capped particle budgets) to ensure smooth frame rates in standard web browsers alongside a clean telemetry HUD,intuitive controls, and full bilingual support.
